title: The Secret to Self-Control
coreMove: Engineer the cue out of reach instead of trying to resist it once it appears

exampleSpecs.domain: a night-shift ICU nurse who keeps reaching for the vending machine cookies stocked next to the staff coffee maker
exampleSpecs.audience: a healthcare worker whose shift wrecks her usual eating rhythm
exampleSpecs.stakes: a creeping ten pounds and an A1C reading her own doctor flagged last month
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she stops trying to white-knuckle past the cookies and instead asks the unit clerk to relocate the basket to the supply room across the hall, and notices the craving fade within a week without any added willpower

exampleSpecs.domain: a recovering sports-betting app user uninstalling the app and asking his bank to block the merchant category
exampleSpecs.audience: a thirty-eight-year-old contractor six weeks into trying to quit
exampleSpecs.stakes: his marriage, after his wife found a hidden card statement
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he chooses friction over discipline by removing the app and the saved payment method, recognizing that every minute the icon was on his phone was a minute he was relying on resolve he did not actually have

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school orchestra teacher rearranging her classroom so the phone charging station is by the door instead of the music stands
exampleSpecs.audience: a teacher tired of confiscating phones mid-rehearsal
exampleSpecs.stakes: twenty-five teenagers losing fifteen minutes of every period to checking notifications
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the rearrangement converts a daily discipline battle into a default; show the room before, the room after, and the visible drop in interruptions without a single new rule

exampleSpecs.domain: a couple arguing about screens at the dinner table while their seven-year-old watches
exampleSpecs.audience: two parents who have each separately resolved to 'be more present'
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether their kid grows up associating dinner with parents staring at their laps
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the conversation moves from blaming each other's self-control to agreeing on a basket by the front door where both phones live from 6pm to 8pm, framing it as a design fix not a moral upgrade

exampleSpecs.domain: a graduate student in molecular biology trying to stop refreshing her advisor's inbox for grant news
exampleSpecs.audience: a PhD candidate three months from her qualifying exam
exampleSpecs.stakes: focused lab time she cannot get back, and sleep she is losing to 2am email checks
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she reviews a wasted week and traces every refresh back to one cue — the email tab pinned in her browser — and concludes the fix is unpinning the tab and signing out on her laptop, not promising herself to check less

exampleSpecs.domain: a former pack-a-day smoker walking past the bodega where he used to buy his cigarettes
exampleSpecs.audience: a man eight months into quitting
exampleSpecs.stakes: a relapse that statistically would set him back to square one
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he notices that the urge is not inside him but inside the route, and quietly changes his walk home to the next street over, treating the rerouting as the actual self-control rather than the gritted teeth he used to call self-control
